# Blaschke cap-area identity and loss of the fiber index

This note tests a surface-area route using the new boundary stress. It
establishes an identity in its stated noncoincidence regime and an exact
obstruction to eliminating fiber labels. It does not prove an OC bound.

The ordinary background is the definition of Blaschke addition by addition
of surface-area measures and the Kneser--Suss inequality. A primary author
source consulted solely for these standard statements is R. J. Gardner,
The Brunn--Minkowski inequality, Section 18.3:
https://sites.stat.washington.edu/jaw/COURSES/520s/523/HO.523.20/Gardner.BullAMS.02.pdf
For d>=2, the inequality is

    |K # L|^((d-1)/d) >= |K|^((d-1)/d)+|L|^((d-1)/d),

with equality precisely for homothetic positive bodies. In dimension two
Blaschke addition equals Minkowski addition up to translation.

## 1. Exact normal-area bookkeeping

Let eta be the sum of the boundary-area measures of positive actual
fibers K_p, marked with their continuous normal. Suppose a selected
critical-cap certificate has nu=sum_j lambda_j 1_(H_j) eta and that
eta and nu have identical normal marginals. Assume here that none of
the selected cap planes contains a positive-area fiber facet. Thus cap
body traces are unambiguous and a zero-volume cap section contributes
no (d-1)-area. Write v_j for its unit continuous cap normal and S_j for
its total proper section area. Then, as measures on the unit sphere,

    sum_j lambda_j sum_p S_(K_p intersect H_j)
       =sum_p S_(K_p)+sum_j lambda_j S_j delta_(-v_j).              (1)

The surface of a proper convex cap consists of the original body
boundary inside the cap and its flat cut face with outward normal
-v_j. Full fibers give their full surface measure; empty fibers give
zero. Summing this elementary decomposition proves (1). The body
portion is exactly the normal marginal of nu, equal to that of eta.
This identity by itself has no positive-volume comparison in the
direction needed to bound beta.

The noncoincidence assumption is explicit. At an outside supporting
facet the general stress uses an allocation sigma, and its surface
contribution is sigma times the pair of opposite facet-normal atoms.
It cannot silently be replaced by the full surface-area measure of
the closed degenerate cap. Any general Blaschke extension must retain
that allocation. No such replacement is used in the example below.

## 2. Sharp OC examples can have arbitrarily large aggregate Blaschke volume

Take n=1,d=2,P={0,1}, and for L>=1 let

    K_0=conv{(0,0),(L,0),(0,1/L)},
    K_1=conv{(0,0),(1/L,0),(0,L)}.

Both triangles have area 1/2. Their lifted convex hull is a genuine
three-dimensional convex body with exactly these two integer fibers,
so its total mixed area is M=1.

At either base p, any continuous halfspace through a candidate can be
extended to an ambient halfspace which excludes the other whole fiber:
choose the integer coefficient of the appropriate sign and sufficiently
large magnitude. Conversely every containing ambient halfspace cuts the
own fiber by a containing continuous halfspace or contains that whole
fiber. It follows exactly that

    depth_S(p,x)=(1/2) depth_(K_p)(x).

The triangle maximum is gamma_2=4/9, attained at its centroid. Hence
this family has exact maximum mixed depth beta=2/9=gamma_2/2 for every
L. The argument includes oblique halfspaces and does not approximate
the integer coefficient by a vertical limiting cap.

In the plane the aggregate Blaschke body B=K_0 # K_1 is their Minkowski
sum up to translation. Its vertices are

    (0,0), (L+1/L,0), (L,L), (0,L+1/L).

For example, this polygon follows by adding the edge vectors in angular
order; the other pairwise vertex sums lie inside it. Its shoelace area
is exactly

    |B|=L^2+1.                                       (2)

Thus |B|/M is unbounded even on exact sharp mixed-depth examples.

There is also an exact compatible cap-area certificate. At each triangle
take the three vertex caps through its centroid, extending each one to
exclude the other fiber as above. Each cap is a translate of (2/3)K_p
and has area 2/9=Q. Give each of the six caps multiplier lambda_j=3/4.
The multiplier sum is 9/2=1/beta. On each original edge, the two incident
vertex caps each cover two thirds of its length; their weighted total
edge length is (3/4)(4/3)=1 times the original length. Consequently the
weighted body-trace normal marginal equals the full boundary normal
marginal, exactly as required in (1).

Each cap's full surface-area measure is (2/3)S_(K_p). Thus their weighted
aggregate surface measure is

    sum_j lambda_j S_(cap_j)=(3/2)(S_(K_0)+S_(K_1)).

Its planar Blaschke body is (3/2)B up to translation, with area

    (9/4)(L^2+1).                                    (3)

Meanwhile the lambda-weighted SUM of cap areas remains exactly
6*(3/4)*(2/9)=1=M. Equations (2)--(3) exhibit explicitly the large
cross-shape contribution that is lost if one confuses a Blaschke
aggregate volume with the sum of its fiber volumes.

Therefore a route that aggregates all fibers into one Blaschke body and
then bounds that body's volume by a dimension-only multiple of M is
false, already at the sharp constant. The Kneser--Suss lower bound has
the opposite direction and cannot supply that missing upper bound.
A useful surface-area route would have to retain the fiber labels or
control the cross-shape terms by an additional proved invariant.
